The trochophore larva of the Atlantic woodeater (Xylonora atlantica) measures just 0.004 cm  in length, a diminutive size that reflects the low-investment reproductive strategy common among iteroparous bivalves. Shortly after cilia-driven feeding commences, the larva develops a calcified shell and transitions into a planktotrophic veliger stage. At this phase, the umboveliger attains a shell height of approximately 0.0135 cm [Lb = approximately 0.0135 cm], representing the size at which the larva begins to allocate resources toward the development of the larval feeding organ. Experiments conducted at a stable water temperature of 12 °C [T = 12 °C] have demonstrated that the interval from gamete fusion to egg hatching is brief, with the age at hatching recorded at 2 days . This rapid embryonic development is typical of species that produce small, yolk-poor eggs. Following eclosion, the endotrophic larva relies on maternally derived reserves for a short period before the mouth opens and first exogenous feeding begins, marking the critical trophic switch from lecithotrophic to planktotrophic nutrition in this species.

Under the same thermal regime of 12 °C [T = 12 °C], the age at birth for Xylonora atlantica is 25 days [ab = 25 days], a value that places the onset of the free-swimming stage later than in many related bivalve species. Laboratory rearing studies indicate that the total time since birth at the end of metamorphosis is 31 days , during which the larva undergoes a complete body plan reorganisation that includes velum loss and gill development at a temperature of 12 °C [T = 12 °C]. The shell height at the end of metamorphosis reaches 0.035 cm , a metric that signals the transition from a pelagic to a benthic existence. Settlement onto suitable substrata occurs when the pediveliger acquires metamorphic competence, a process that is strongly influenced by local environmental cues. After this morphological transformation, the post-metamorphic juvenile, or spat, begins feeding on phytoplankton and benthic microalgae, initiating a sustained period of somatic growth that will continue for several months.

Sexual maturation in the Atlantic woodeater is reached when individuals attain a shell height of 0.2 cm [Lp = 0.2 cm], a size threshold that coincides with the onset of gametogenesis. The corresponding wet weight at puberty is 0.004 grams [Wwp = 0.004 grams], a modest mass that reflects the species' small adult body size. Field records indicate that the time since birth at puberty is 108 days [tp = 108 days] when water temperatures remain near 12 °C [T = 12 °C]; this interval corresponds roughly to 74 days after the completion of settlement and metamorphosis. Comparative data from congeneric species suggest that this developmental timeline is accelerated relative to cold-water specialists, likely because elevated temperatures promote faster metabolic rates and more rapid attainment of the critical body size required for reproductive activation. The relatively short pre-pubertal period may also reflect selection pressures linked to the seasonal availability of phytoplankton blooms in the species' coastal habitat.

Reproduction in Xylonora atlantica is characterised by a maximum reproductive rate achieved under near-freezing conditions. At a water temperature of 4 °C [T = 4 °C], females produce approximately 11 eggs per spawning event [N_R_i = approximately 11 eggs per spawning event] and can complete up to 6 spawning events annually [F_R_i = up to 6 spawning events annually]. This high fecundity is unusual for a bivalve of its size and may represent an adaptation to the unpredictability of food resources in the boreal Atlantic waters it inhabits. The ultimate shell height attained by adults is 1.5 cm [Li = 1.5 cm], placing the species among the smaller members of its family. This diminutive final size constrains the volume of the mantle cavity and, consequently, the maximum gonad mass that can be accommodated, yet the species compensates through a high spawning frequency. Gonad maturation appears to be synchronised with seasonal temperature cycles, with peak spawning activity occurring during the coldest months when planktonic predators are less abundant.

Longevity data for Atlantic woodeater come from mark-recapture studies conducted in subtidal populations off the coast of Nova Scotia. The maximum recorded lifespan is 547 days [am = 547 days] at a mean water temperature of 8 °C [T = 8 °C], a duration that is typical for small, fast-growing bivalves with high annual reproductive output. Senescence in this species is characterised by progressive deterioration of the ctenidia and a gradual decline in filtration efficiency, leading to a negative energy balance in older individuals. The relationship between temperature and lifespan is inverse: individuals from warmer microhabitats tend to mature earlier but also succumb to age-related mortality sooner than those from colder refugia. Ecological mortality from predation by naticid gastropods and decapod crustaceans further truncates the realised lifespan in the wild, with few individuals reaching the physiological maximum. This life-history syndrome—rapid growth, early maturity, high fecundity, and short lifespan—positions Xylonora atlantica as a classic r-selected species within its benthic community.
